The (simple) LED circuit

First we want to show one of the simplest possible circuits, some that lighten your day (or night, pun intdnded).

item.title: Storytelling and the order of things
item.description:
Storytelling and the order of things

Hey reader,

today I want to talk with you about the (right) order of things and its importance. When creating my first blog articles about electronics I hit multiple times the same obstacle, which is the order of things.

When trying to teach people about one of my favourite things I almost over the same amount of time, I am thinking about the educational purpose to the reader. That happened to me years ago, when I started this blog, and its happened to me ever since in a regular manner. So, for the existing blog posts, I came up with the following order (starting with linear components): (1) Resistors, then (2) capacitors and its counterpart coils, then - as last group, (3) - all the nonlinear components. Last but not least we want to discuss integrated circuits (IC) which are made of all components before - with exception to the coils which are hardly to made up in silicon. For the nonlinear components I will also try to get an educational purposeful order, so we want start here with the LED, then get to normal diodes then to (MOSFET) transistors…​

item.description:
Time-sensitive components

After reviewing and extensively describing the most important component, the resistor, in the first part, now we want to have a look at the next important component, the capacitor. Capacitor are also passive components, meaning they do not amplify a signal.

Electrostatic field

If we take two metal planes and park them side by side, with a small thin layer of a non-conducting substance in-between, we created an electrostatic field.

item.title: How does a CPU work? Overview
item.description:
How does a CPU work – Table of Contents

Introduction and Overview

Introduction and Overview

Each topic in this course is divided into two parts: one focusing on the mathematical side of digital logic— ideally independent of implementation details— and another more concrete part dealing with those very details. In the concrete part, we will mostly discuss implementations on the electrical level, although other solutions are possible, such as those based on fluid dynamics or optical gates.
